sentences: On a Sunday afternoon, Parisians dance and chat at an open-air dance hall on the hill of Montmartre.
This is Renoir's Bal du moulin de la Galette, painted in 1876.
You can almost hear the band.
This was a place where working-class Parisians came to dance, drink and eat galettes, a kind of flat cake.
Renoir worked on this large canvas close to the actual spot and posed his friends as models.
According to his friend Georges Rivière, Renoir rented a studio nearby on the rue Cortot and painted the canvas on the spot.
Some days, Rivière remembered, the wind threatened to carry the whole canvas away.
Up above, round lamps hang in rows among the branches of the trees.
What makes the picture come alive is not the people but the light, and that light comes filtered down to us through the leaves.
Now look deeper into the picture.
Further back, the dancers dissolve into the crowd behind them.
By keeping the front sharp and the back blurred, Renoir gives us the depth of the wide dance floor and even a sense of its noise and bustle.
Look at the woman in the pink dress dancing on the left.
Sunlight filtered through the leaves scatters in patches of pink and yellow across clothes, faces and the ground.
Even her partner's dark suit catches the light.
The bright spots on the ground are the same dappled light.
Here Impressionism's method of softening outlines and building light from flecks of color is used in its most joyful form.
The whole floor glitters.
The woman in the striped dress in front is Estelle, the sister of Jeanne Samary, Renoir's favourite young model.
Behind her, another woman leans in with a hand on her shoulder, telling her something.
Around the table on the right sit Renoir's painter friends Franc-Lamy and Goeneutte, along with Rivière, who later wrote about these days.
Little pieces of sunlight sparkle on the dark jacket of the man with his back to us, and on the glasses.
The painter Gustave Caillebotte owned this canvas, and after his death it passed to the French state.
It now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, and Renoir also painted a smaller version with the same title.
You can almost hear the music, laughter and dancing feet; it is a lively portrait that celebrates modern city people at their leisure.
If you could step into this dance hall, where in the crowd would you choose to sit?
